video_title: Michelle Knudsen: Rebuilding the NYU Endowment from a Clean Sheet of Paper
gist: Michelle Knudsen, CIO of the NYU endowment since mid-2024, details a ground-up rebuild of an ~$8B pool that was under-allocated to privates (<15%), had almost no venture, and was managed conservatively through the investment committee — turning over a third of the book in two years, pushing equity (public+private) to ~65% and a leverage-heavy absolute-return sleeve toward ~25%, and adding venture and lower-mid-market buyout precisely while peers retrench. The operating edge is governance (3% manager-size trigger for IC sign-off, IC input pulled to the front of diligence, team debate moved to 70% through research) rather than market calls, with her named risks being private-market fundraising FOMO and public markets underpricing the medium-term impact of private markets and AI.

insights.claim: The NYU endowment stands at roughly $8 billion today, up from a little over $6 billion when Michelle Knudsen took the CIO seat in 2024, and was a sub-$2 billion pool as recently as 2010 — making it far younger and smaller relative to its institution than most peer endowments.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A young, fast-growing endowment with a growth mandate is a rising source of new LP capital — GPs raising funds should treat NYU as a genuinely new allocator rather than a stable incumbent LP with fixed relationships.
insights.quote: NYU's portfolio today is um just about 8 billion.

insights.claim: NYU has turned over a little more than a third of its portfolio in the past two years and re-underwritten roughly another third, meaning about two-thirds of the book has been actively touched since the CIO transition.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Sizeable manager turnover at an $8B pool implies both real redemption flows out of incumbent managers and live mandates being awarded — a mapping exercise worth doing for anyone selling to endowments.
insights.quote: We've turned over a little more than a third of it in the last two years and we've rewritten probably about another third of it.

insights.claim: The pre-2024 NYU portfolio was almost entirely bottom-up fundamental, mostly US corporate securities (largely equity, some credit) with every investment decision routed through the investment committee and an explicit volatility-management objective — a structure Knudsen says had to be rebuilt end-to-end once the mandate shifted to growth.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Illustrates that a 'conservative' endowment posture is usually a governance artifact, not a market view; when university leadership changes the return mandate, the whole factor profile of the portfolio changes with it.

insights.claim: Knudsen argues the way to win credibility with an investment committee during a rebuild is speed of visible execution — NYU had a new governance structure, a new asset allocation framework, and had begun re-underwriting every line item within three months of her arrival.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A template for any new CIO or PM inheriting a book: front-load structural decisions in the first quarter to buy discretion for the multi-year plan, rather than sequencing changes gradually.
insights.quote: It started with a plan of action on how to create a plan of action.

insights.claim: The portfolio's risk and return profile has been deliberately diversified away from homogeneity — quant exposure, macro and relative-value hedge fund strategies, and venture capital have all been added where they were previously absent or minimal.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Signals demand from a large new LP for quant, macro/RV and venture products specifically — categories that had no prior representation in this book.

insights.claim: NYU set an explicit 3% of portfolio threshold above which any manager allocation requires investment committee buy-in, while leaving all manager selection below that level with the investment team.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable governance rule: place the decision at the level with the most information and reserve committee escalation for positions large enough to be a real concentration of risk.
insights.quote: We set that level at 3%.

insights.claim: Knudsen deliberately escalates to the investment committee before hitting the 3% line rather than optimizing around it, and says the committee's questions in the handful of escalations have centered on how a levered manager affects portfolio-wide leverage and on the manager's role in the portfolio — not on the manager pick itself.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Shows the escalation is functioning as intended — committees add value on portfolio-level risk aggregation, and CIOs who treat thresholds as ceilings to game lose that benefit.

insights.claim: NYU pulled investment committee input to the very beginning of the research process by presenting a long-list pipeline of names most of which will never be funded, on the argument that late-stage committee input arrives too late to change any outcome.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Extracts the committee's manager network and objections as diligence inputs rather than as end-stage vetoes — an allocation-process design worth importing anywhere a board holds relevant knowledge.
insights.quote: I think too often we wait until the last minute to get information that could have actually changed the outcome had we gotten it earlier.

insights.claim: The investment committee's remit was narrowed to direction-setting — risk levels and frameworks for initiatives like standing up a co-investment portfolio or executing secondary sales — which Knudsen says the committee found a relief rather than a loss of control.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: The framework-first governance model lets an office run co-invest and secondary programs at speed without per-deal board approval — a prerequisite for competing on those timelines.

themes.theme: Equity Beta as the Universal Hurdle Rate

insights.claim: NYU's allocation framework treats long-term equity market exposure as the most reliable source of return and forces every single investment in the portfolio to justify itself against that benchmark, with explicit stated reasons required for any deviation from equity beta.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A hurdle-rate discipline that mechanically disfavors low-return diversifiers; applied broadly it explains why endowments are shrinking fixed income and real assets sleeves.
insights.quote: the most reliable source of return over the long term is equity market exposure

insights.claim: NYU's target structure is roughly 65% equity (public plus private), an absolute return and opportunistic bucket being built toward roughly 25%, and a relatively small residual across cash, fixed income and real estate.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A 25% absolute-return target at an $8B pool implies roughly $2B of hedge fund demand being built out — a meaningful ticket source for the strategies she favors.

insights.claim: Knudsen says real assets is a heavily debated allocation internally at NYU, with an open question over whether the sleeve deserves a dedicated allocation at all.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: If sophisticated endowments are questioning whether real assets is a standalone bucket rather than a set of opportunistic trades, that is a structural headwind for dedicated real-asset fundraising.

insights.claim: NYU runs a hybrid between traditional asset allocation and a total portfolio approach — grouping assets by the role they play, then applying an explicit criteria list to every investment to determine which bucket it belongs in.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Role-based bucketing with per-investment criteria is what lets an allocator hold unconventional strategies (royalties, asset-backed finance) without breaking the policy portfolio.

themes.theme: High-Octane Hedge Funds and Contagion Sizing

insights.claim: Almost all of NYU's absolute return and opportunistic bucket is currently in trading-oriented hedge fund strategies running higher levels of leverage, where the return source is manager skill, technology or data insight rather than a single persistent risk premium.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Concentrating an entire 25%-target sleeve in skill-and-leverage-based strategies is a bet that alpha capacity is available at scale — and makes the sleeve highly sensitive to a multi-manager deleveraging event.

insights.claim: Knudsen says NYU could only lean into leveraged trading strategies because it hired a team with deep expertise in those strategies first — the underwriting capability was a precondition for the allocation, not a consequence of it.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Explains why most endowments cannot simply copy a multi-strategy/quant tilt: the constraint is internal underwriting talent, so allocations to these strategies follow specific senior hires.

insights.claim: NYU explicitly models common-investor risk and correlations rising toward one in stress scenarios, and sizes the total leveraged hedge fund exposure so the portfolio survives all managers hitting their bad case simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: The sizing rule — survive the simultaneous worst case rather than the diversified one — is the practical answer to multi-manager crowding risk and caps how big the sleeve can get.
insights.quote: we size the total portfolio so that if we get that bad case scenario across all of our managers at the same time, we can live with it.

insights.claim: Knudsen deliberately runs stress-correlation analysis separately from day-to-day return correlation expectations, because looking only at stress scenarios would cause the portfolio to take too little risk in normal times.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A useful correction to tail-risk-dominated risk frameworks: separating the two lenses prevents chronic under-risking, which is itself a permanent drag on an endowment's spend-plus-inflation target.

themes.theme: Counter-Cyclical Privates and the Venture Catch-Up

insights.claim: Less than 15% of the NYU endowment was in private assets when Knudsen arrived, and NYU has been growing that allocation substantially while many peer endowments have been cutting theirs.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A large, liquid, under-allocated LP scaling into privates during a peer-group retrenchment is buying at a moment of weak competition for allocations — and is a natural buyer in the LP secondaries market.
insights.quote: we have the ability and we have been growing that portfolio pretty substantially over the last few years when many of our peers have been pulling back their allocations

insights.claim: NYU had very little venture capital exposure before 2024 and prioritized building it specifically because Knudsen joined as the early years of AI were kicking off and wanted that exposure in the portfolio.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Confirms institutional venture demand is being underwritten explicitly as AI exposure — meaning venture fundraising conditions are tied to the AI cycle's perceived durability, not to venture returns broadly.

insights.claim: NYU built its venture program as a barbell across the full spectrum — from incubator and pre-seed through pre-IPO companies now going public — using a mix of large multi-stage firms and smaller boutiques, with the boutiques valued for exposure to mid-size companies that are plausible acquisition targets for the megacaps rather than only moonshots.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: The explicit M&A-exit thesis for smaller venture positions suggests LPs are underwriting acquisition by large AI incumbents as a primary liquidity path, not just IPOs.

insights.claim: NYU is targeting lower-mid-market buyout specifically because public market concentration means the buyout book can act as diversification within the overall equity bucket rather than as a return enhancer alone.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Reframes small buyout as a factor hedge against megacap concentration — a rationale that supports lower-mid-market fundraising even as large-cap buyout faces LP fatigue.

insights.claim: Knudsen positions NYU's institutional footprint — largest private university in the US, 60,000 students, 700,000 living alumni, plus NYU Langone Medical Center — as the LP's competitive currency for accessing capacity-constrained venture and private equity managers, alongside team-level service like same-day responsiveness during manager crises.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Access to top-decile private managers is being won on relationship and institutional affinity, not price — a structural disadvantage for allocators without a brand or a service culture.
insights.quote: We have 60,000 students, 700,000 living alumni

insights.claim: Knudsen treats backward-looking track record data as a question-generator rather than a decision input, deliberately hunting for the places where a manager's historical portfolio behavior contradicts their stated forward vision.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A repeatable diligence method: the alpha in reference data is in the gaps between narrative and history, not in the returns series itself.
insights.quote: it should be the impetus to ask questions but not the basis on which we should make decisions

insights.claim: Knudsen says NYU spends more time than her prior seats on interrogating why an opportunity set exists at all and why it should persist, because an endowment of NYU's size is not obligated to allocate to any particular strategy.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Optionality to do nothing is the mid-size allocator's real edge over mega-endowments that must deploy — it permits skipping crowded opportunity sets entirely.

insights.claim: Knudsen flags a rise in mismatches in recent years between the duration of an opportunity set and the fund structure a manager wraps around it, and screens explicitly to ensure the vehicle actually delivers the exposure being underwritten.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A warning on product engineering in private markets — evergreen and semi-liquid wrappers around illiquid opportunity sets are a specific failure mode to diligence, and a source of future LP disappointment.

insights.claim: Knudsen says her natural bias is toward managers with articulate process, but explicitly disciplines it because process does not necessarily produce returns — while arguing endowment portfolios under-weight portfolio-construction thinking in favor of individual security stories.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A named self-bias worth borrowing: a compelling investment process is a comfort signal, not evidence of edge, and should be scored separately from expected return.
insights.quote: process doesn't necessarily yield returns

insights.claim: In underwriting people, Knudsen argues small two-or-three-person teams are easier to read but more fragile, while large firms require mapping decision-making structures and multiple decision-makers' mindsets yet are usually more stable because one person's impact is buffered by scale.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A direct trade-off framework for emerging-manager versus platform allocations: legibility versus key-person durability, priced differently at each end of the size spectrum.

themes.theme: Public Markets Bifurcation and Regime Shift Risks

insights.claim: Knudsen sees public markets bifurcating between passive flows, systematic and quantitative strategies, a large retail component, and very long-horizon fundamental managers — and argues the opportunity sits in the underpopulated middle, trading around short-term volatility while underwriting medium-to-long-term company outcomes.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Names a specific under-supplied strategy niche where an allocator is actively writing tickets — medium-horizon, volatility-aware fundamental equity.

insights.claim: Knudsen argues managers accessing that middle-ground public equity opportunity must be size-constrained to stay nimble, making capacity discipline a screening criterion rather than a nice-to-have.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Implies persistent LP demand for small and mid-size equity managers that cap assets — and structural difficulty for scaled long-only shops competing for the same mandate.
insights.quote: asset managers who can be more nimble, which means they have to be size constrained

insights.claim: Knudsen names her biggest public-markets risk as investors underappreciating the medium-to-long-term impact of private markets and of AI, with uncertainty over where recent public market repricing has thrown out babies with the bathwater versus where the coming changes are not yet recognized at all.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A CIO stress-testing public equity factor exposure for AI disruption implies allocators are beginning to treat AI displacement as a portfolio factor, not a sector call.
insights.quote: I think the risks are that we're underappreciating the impact of private markets and of AI over the medium to long term

insights.claim: Knudsen distinguishes the end of the zero interest rate environment as a regime shift requiring strategic reallocation from ordinary volatility and rotating six-month leadership in concentrated stock groups, which she classifies as noise to be crowded out.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: The regime-versus-noise filter determines what actually changes an allocation; rate normalization flowing through asset classes is being treated as a multi-year strategic input, not a tactical one.
insights.quote: Some of it has to do with figuring out how the end of the zero interest rate environment really flows through to different asset classes, right? And that's more of a regime shift rather than temporary volatility.

insights.claim: Knudsen identifies a persistently aggressive private-markets fundraising cycle as a top risk, specifically that FOMO drives over-commitment, and has responded by building out commitment pacing models with sector-specific critical questions.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Even an LP actively increasing its private allocation is bracing against over-commitment — a signal that pacing discipline, not appetite, will govern the next leg of private fundraising.
insights.quote: fear of missing out will propel us to invest in uh more of it than we should

insights.claim: NYU moved its main team debate on a prospective investment to roughly 70% through the research process instead of at the end, on the theory that a team challenges assumptions more usefully — and a deal team defends less — when there is still real diligence left to run.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A transferable fix for the end-stage-approval failure mode in any investment committee: move the challenge point before the team is psychologically committed.
insights.quote: We moved the big team discussion to that stage because that's where we want the benefit of the team's power to question some of the assumptions

insights.claim: NYU's investment team has grown to 12 people across investment and operations, with 10 of the 12 new since June 2024, built by hiring a private-markets MD and an absolute-return MD with deep strategy-specific expertise before scaling those allocations.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: The hiring sequence is the leading indicator of allocation shifts — a senior hire in a strategy predicts capital flowing into that strategy 12-24 months later.
insights.quote: 10 of the 12 are new since June of 2024.

insights.claim: NYU protects a weekly research-only team meeting that is never cancelled — defaulting to a macro discussion when no specific topic exists — on the argument that the team's edge comes from pooling the different information streams each member absorbs, and that written notes or a research management system cannot substitute for in-room debate.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: An operational detail with compounding effects: mandatory, undroppable synthesis time is how small teams compete with larger, longer-established allocators.
insights.quote: we're all taking in such different information and the power of the team is in pulling that all together

insights.claim: NYU is deploying AI tools operationally — Claude and Gemini to reformat raw notes, Granola and Whisperflow for capture — and is undertaking a project to mine managers' audited financial statements as a time series to track how individual funds evolve across the portfolio, work previously done only one-off by hand.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of AI adoption inside institutional allocators at the information-aggregation layer, and a specific emerging use case — longitudinal analysis of fund audited financials — that could commoditize a manual LP diligence advantage.
insights.quote: whether it's using claude or Gemini to take raw notes and put them into something that is a format we can all consume or using granola or whisperflow to capture thoughts

insights.claim: NYU stood up a co-investment portfolio earlier this year and is deliberately running it at a crawl, with the two-year goal only to reach a walk — an explicitly paced approach to a structure many allocators scale quickly.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: A new co-invest program at an $8B endowment is incremental deal flow demand for GPs, but the deliberate pacing means capacity will be modest for several years.
insights.quote: We stood up a co-investment portfolio earlier this year and I would say we're we're crawling with it right now.

insights.claim: NYU's next phase is building nuanced risk management at the sleeve level — for the equity sleeve and the absolute return sleeve individually — rather than only at the total portfolio level where its current risk work sits.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Sleeve-level risk systems are a precondition for running higher-leverage strategies at scale; it signals the absolute-return bucket has more room to grow once the plumbing exists.

insights.claim: Knudsen argues investors systematically over-invest in the initial allocation decision and under-invest in forcing a good outcome afterward, holding that the decision to exit, to decline a re-up, or to re-up is as important as the original commitment.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Reframes LP work as ongoing outcome management rather than selection — implying underperformance in endowment portfolios is often a monitoring and exit-discipline failure, not a selection failure.
insights.quote: if we stop at the decision, then we've we've we've abdicated our responsibility

insights.claim: Knudsen's core risk heuristic, formed by graduating into the 2008 crisis at Goldman Sachs, is that you must be able to articulate and pre-plan for the bad case even if you dislike it, because decision-making on the fly amid fast-changing information is where investors fail.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: The pre-committed downside plan is what distinguishes the managers who survive drawdowns; it is also a diligence question to put to any levered manager.
insights.quote: I don't have to like the downside scenario, but I have to be able to live with it.

insights.claim: Knudsen credits the commercial pressure of the OCIO model — where a for-profit asset manager has no automatic right to exist — as the mindset that transfers most powerfully into endowment investing, where smart people hold very stable jobs and are less forced to innovate on portfolio construction and net-of-fee returns.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: An implied critique of endowment complacency: job security removes the forcing function for fee and structure innovation, which is where OCIO-trained allocators can find edge.
insights.quote: when you're at an OCIO or a for-profit asset management firm, you have no right to exist.

insights.claim: Knudsen says Partners Capital was pushed into underwriting emerging managers and fund ones not by preference but by capacity constraints at its existing managers as AUM grew from about $6 billion to $30 billion — and NYU has since backed a fund one, a new-launch hedge fund and a couple of fund twos in two years.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Emerging-manager allocation is driven mechanically by incumbent capacity limits at growing LPs, meaning fund-one demand rises with allocator AUM growth rather than with market sentiment.

insights.claim: Knudsen notes that fiduciary investment committees at foundations and endowments displayed lower risk appetite than the private equity GPs who were Partners Capital's private clients, driven by sensitivity to a December 31 mark that sets the spend level.
insights.speaker: Michelle Knudsen
insights.so_what: Explains a persistent structural bias: institutional risk tolerance is set by the reporting-date spend mechanism, not by the true investment horizon — which is precisely the arbitrage a long-horizon endowment can exploit.
